record.paper_title: Eight Open Problems in Distributed Computing
record.original_question: For randomized wait-free consensus against a weak adversary that cannot observe private coin flips before they are made public, where an O(log n) per-process work protocol is known using multi-writer registers, can one prove a nontrivial lower bound, ideally an Omega(log n) lower bound, for multi-writer registers or even for stronger objects such as unit-cost snapshots?

evidence.quote: With a weaker adversary that cannot observe coin flips that have not yet been made public, consensus can be solved in O(log n) work per process using multi-writer registers [11]. There is no corresponding non-trivial lower bound.
It would be interesting to see if an Omega(log n) lower bound could be proved for multi-writer registers or even with strong objects like unit-cost snapshots.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the standard asynchronous shared-memory model with n processes that communicate via atomic registers. The (binary or multi-valued) consensus problem requires each process to start with an input value, eventually decide a value, such that all decisions agree (Agreement), every decided value was some process's input (Validity), and every nonfaulty process eventually decides (Termination, here in the wait-free sense: any number of processes may fail by crashing). Algorithms may be randomized, with each process tossing private local coins, and the cost measure is per-process work (i.e., the worst-case expected number of shared-memory steps performed by a single process). The scheduling is controlled by an adversary; here the adversary is "weak" in the sense that it cannot observe the outcome of a coin flip until that outcome has been written to a shared register (i.e., made public).

It is known that under such a weak adversary, randomized wait-free consensus is solvable with O(log n) expected work per process using multi-writer atomic registers. 

Problem: Prove a nontrivial lower bound on the per-process expected work for randomized wait-free consensus among n processes against a weak adversary that cannot observe coin flips before they are made public, in the shared-memory model with multi-writer atomic registers (and, more generally, with stronger primitives such as unit-cost atomic snapshot objects). Ideally, establish a matching Ω(log n) per-process lower bound, or otherwise show any superconstant lower bound in these models.
artifact.category_tag: distributed computing / randomized consensus lower bounds
artifact.status_search_result: Existing lower bounds for randomized consensus under weak/oblivious adversaries (Attiya–Censor; later work) address termination-probability versus total step complexity tradeoffs and Ω(n) register-count bounds, but no nontrivial per-process work lower bound (let alone Ω(log n)) for multi-writer registers or unit-cost snapshots against a weak adversary appears in the literature. Upper bounds have actually improved (e.g., O(log log n) per step expected with multi-writer registers under an oblivious adversary), widening the gap. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Lower Bounds for Randomized Consensus under a Weak Adversary
status_evidence.snippet: Lower bound concerns the probability of non-termination within k(n−f) steps, not per-process work in multi-writer registers.
status_evidence.claim: Existing weak-adversary lower bounds target termination probability vs. total steps, not per-process Ω(log n).

status_evidence.title: Faster randomized consensus with an oblivious adversary
status_evidence.snippet: Achieves O(log log n + log(1/μ)) steps with multi-writer registers against an oblivious adversary.
status_evidence.claim: Upper bounds for weak/oblivious adversaries have improved; no matching nontrivial per-process lower bound is known.

status_evidence.title: Consensus with Max Registers (DISC 2019)
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses consensus algorithms and complexity using stronger objects.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work continues to improve upper bounds; corresponding nontrivial lower bounds for unit-cost snapshots/multi-writer registers under weak adversaries are not established.
